name: Dimethylpolysiloxane
text:
Dimethylpolysiloxane is a synthetic silicone polymer, a clear, odourless, oily liquid made from silicon, oxygen and methyl groups. It is not found in nature.

In food it works as an anti-foaming agent and anti-caking agent. It stops foam forming during cooking and processing, for example in frying oils, jams, soft drinks and fruit juices.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods and approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for food packaging.

name: Beeswax
text:
Beeswax is a natural wax secreted by honeybees to build honeycomb. It is collected during honey processing and comes as white or yellow wax, depending on whether it has been bleached.

In food it is used as a glazing agent, giving a protective shiny coating to confectionery, fruit and some tablets, and it is also used to coat cheese rinds.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK and approved in the US. It is not suitable for strict vegans because it is an animal product.

name: Candelilla wax
text:
Candelilla wax is a natural plant wax obtained from the leaves of the candelilla shrub, which grows in northern Mexico and the south-western United States.

It serves as a glazing agent, giving a hard, glossy finish. It is used in chewing gum bases, hard candies and as a coating on some confectionery.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods and approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for chewing gum and hard candy.

name: Carnauba wax
text:
Carnauba wax is a hard natural wax collected from the leaves of the carnauba palm, which grows in north-eastern Brazil. It is known for its high melting point and strong shine.

As a glazing agent it is used to polish confectionery such as dragees and chocolate-coated sweets, to coat fresh fruit and in chewing gum.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods and approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for certain foods.

name: Shellac
text:
Shellac is a natural resin secreted by the lac insect, which lives on trees in India and Thailand. The resin is scraped off, purified and sometimes bleached, and is sold as flakes.

In food it is used as a glazing agent to give a glossy, protective coating to confectionery, tablets, food supplements and the skin of some fruit such as apples and citrus.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods, approved in the UK and approved in the US. As an insect product it is not vegan.

name: Microcrystalline wax
text:
Microcrystalline wax is a refined wax made from petroleum. It consists of a mixture of saturated hydrocarbons and is more flexible and finer-grained than ordinary paraffin wax.

In practice such waxes are used as coatings and surface treatments, for example on cheese rinds and some fruit, and in chewing gum bases.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods and approved in the UK. It is not approved in the US under this listing.

name: High viscosity mineral oils
text:
Mineral oils are highly refined mixtures of liquid hydrocarbons derived from petroleum. High viscosity grades are thick, colourless, tasteless and odourless.

They are used as anti-foaming agents and as release or coating agents, for example in confectionery and on dried fruit.

They are approved in the EU for certain foods, not approved in the UK, and approved in the US. Only highly purified food-grade oils are suitable for food use.

name: Petrolatum
text:
Petrolatum, better known as petroleum jelly or Vaseline, is a semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons obtained by refining petroleum. It is odourless and water-repellent.

It is used in small amounts as a release or protective coating agent, for example in baking and confectionery.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved for certain foods.

name: Petroleum wax
text:
Petroleum wax is a group of waxes obtained by refining crude oil. It covers microcrystalline wax and paraffin wax, which are mixtures of saturated hydrocarbons and are solid at room temperature.

They are used as glazing agents, for example as coatings for cheese, fruit and confectionery, and in chewing gum bases.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US, petroleum and paraffin waxes are approved for certain foods.

name: Gum benzoic
text:
Gum benzoic, or benzoin resin, is an aromatic resin obtained from the bark of Styrax trees growing in South-East Asia. It has a sweet, vanilla-like scent and is also used in perfumery and incense.

It is classed as a flavour enhancer, though it has seen little use in modern food production.

It is not approved in the EU, the UK or the US.

name: Hydrogenated poly-1-decene
text:
Hydrogenated poly-1-decene is a synthetic, wax-like hydrocarbon polymer made from the petrochemical 1-decene. It is chemically stable and almost insoluble in water.

It is used as a glazing agent, forming a thin protective shine on products such as confectionery and chewing gum.

It is approved in the EU for certain foods and approved in the UK. It is not approved in the US.

name: Rice bran wax
text:
Rice bran wax is a natural vegetable wax extracted from the oil of rice bran, the outer layer of rice grains, which is a by-product of rice milling.

It is used as a glazing agent to give a shiny coating to confectionery, chewing gum and fresh fruit and vegetables, and helps retain moisture.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved for chewing gum, candy and fresh fruit and vegetables.

name: Spermaceti wax
text:
Spermaceti is a waxy substance obtained from the head cavity of the sperm whale. It was used historically in candles, cosmetics and ointments.

It is listed as a glazing agent, but because of whale conservation and the availability of other waxes it is not used in modern food production.

It is not approved in the EU, the UK or the US.

name: Wax esters
text:
Wax esters are esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain alcohols. They occur naturally in many plant and animal waxes and can also be produced synthetically.

They are classed as glazing agents, meaning coatings that give a shiny, protective surface.

They are not approved in the EU, the UK or the US. Little further information is available for this additive.

name: Methyl esters of fatty acids
text:
Methyl esters of fatty acids are compounds made by reacting fatty acids from vegetable or animal fats with methanol. They are oily liquids.

They are listed as glazing agents. In the US they are permitted in the processing of raisins, where they help the fruit dry and keep a glossy surface.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK, and are approved in the US for raisin making.

name: Montanic acid esters
text:
Montanic acid esters are derived from montan wax, a hard fossil wax extracted from certain types of lignite (brown coal). The wax is refined and esterified to give a stable product.

They are used as glazing agents, mainly as a protective coating for the peel of citrus fruit.

They are approved in the EU, not approved in the UK, and approved in the US as a coating for citrus fruit.

name: Lanolin
text:
Lanolin, or wool grease, is a waxy substance secreted by sheep and recovered during the washing of raw wool. After purification it is a yellowish, sticky wax widely used in cosmetics and skin creams.

It is listed as a glazing agent and has little use in modern foods.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and in the US it is approved for food packaging only.

name: Oxidized polyethylene wax
text:
Oxidized polyethylene wax is a synthetic wax made by partially oxidizing polyethylene, the common plastic. It is a hard, water-resistant solid.

It is used as a glazing agent, mainly as a protective, shiny coating on the peel of certain fruit such as citrus fruit.

It is approved in the EU as a coating for certain fruits only, approved in the UK, and approved in the US as a coating for certain fruit.

name: Esters of colophony
text:
Colophony, also called rosin, is a resin obtained from pine trees. Esters of colophony are made by reacting it with alcohols such as glycerol, which makes a harder and more stable resin.

They are listed as glazing agents and are used, among other things, in chewing gum bases.

They are not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US, colophony is approved for food packaging only.

name: Calcium iodate
text:
Calcium iodate is an inorganic salt of iodic acid, a white powder that contains iodine and acts as an oxidizing agent.

Iodates have been used as flour improvers that strengthen dough, and as a source of iodine.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved for use in bread.

name: Potassium iodate
text:
Potassium iodate is an inorganic salt containing iodine, a white crystalline powder and a strong oxidizing agent. It is made industrially.

It has been used as a flour treatment agent in baking and as a source of iodine for iodized salt in some countries.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and is approved in the US for bread.

name: Nitrogen oxides
text:
Nitrogen oxides are gaseous compounds of nitrogen and oxygen produced industrially. Some of them are toxic, irritating gases, so the term covers substances needing careful handling.

A typical use is as a propellant.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved as a propellant.

name: Nitrosyl chloride
text:
Nitrosyl chloride is a toxic, reactive yellow gas made industrially from nitrogen oxides and chlorine. It is a strong oxidizing and bleaching agent.

It has been described as a flour treatment agent, but it is not used in modern food production.

It is not approved in the EU, the UK or the US.

name: L-cysteine
text:
L-cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid found in proteins. For food use it is obtained by fermentation or by hydrolysis of keratin-rich material such as feathers or hair.

It works as a dough improver, making dough softer and easier to handle in bread, biscuits and flour products.

It is approved in the EU for biscuits and flour, approved in the UK, and approved in the US for dough and baked goods.

name: L-cystine
text:
L-cystine is an amino acid formed from two cysteine molecules joined by a sulfur bridge. It occurs naturally in proteins such as hair and wool, and is a white crystalline powder.

It is listed as an improving agent for flour, but is mainly known as a nutrient supplement.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved as a nutrient.

name: Potassium persulfate
text:
Potassium persulfate is an inorganic salt, a white crystalline powder and a strong oxidizing agent made industrially.

It is listed as a flour improving agent. It is also used as a bleaching and polymerisation agent in industry.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved as a coating on citrus fruit and for food packaging only.

name: Ammonium persulfate
text:
Ammonium persulfate is an inorganic salt, a white crystalline powder that is a strong oxidizing agent. It is produced industrially.

It is listed as a flour improving agent that strengthens dough. It is also used in industry for bleaching and etching.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and is approved in the US.

name: Potassium bromate
text:
Potassium bromate is an inorganic salt, a white crystalline powder and a strong oxidizing agent. It was widely used as a flour improver to strengthen dough and increase loaf volume.

It is listed as an improving agent. It has been restricted because it is considered a potential carcinogen.

It is not approved in the EU and UK for this reason. In the US it is approved for the malting of barley.

name: Calcium bromate
text:
Calcium bromate is an inorganic salt of bromic acid and a strong oxidizing agent. It is made industrially and is related to potassium bromate.

It is listed as an improving agent, used historically to strengthen flour and dough in baking.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Chlorine
text:
Chlorine is a greenish-yellow toxic gas that occurs naturally only in compounds. It is produced industrially, mostly from salt.

It is listed as a preservative, bleach and improving agent. It has been used to bleach and treat flour and, more widely, to disinfect water.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and is approved in the US.

name: Chlorine dioxide
text:
Chlorine dioxide is a yellow-green gas with a strong oxidizing action, made industrially. It is used as a bleach and disinfectant, notably for treating drinking water.

In food it is listed as a bleach, used for flour treatment.

It is approved in the EU and not approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for treating water.

name: Azodicarbonamide
text:
Azodicarbonamide is a synthetic yellow-orange powder. It is used as a flour improver that bleaches the flour and strengthens dough, and also as a foaming agent in plastics.

It is listed as an improving agent for bread and flour.

It has been identified as a Substance of Very High Concern in the EU and is not approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for flour and bread.

name: Carbamide
text:
Carbamide, better known as urea, is a simple nitrogen compound that is produced by the body and excreted in urine. The industrial product is made synthetically.

It is listed as an improving agent. It is used in chewing gum and in some yeast-based products as a nitrogen source.

It is approved in the EU for chewing gum and not approved in the UK. In the US it is approved for baked goods, alcohol and gelatin products.

name: Benzoyl peroxide
text:
Benzoyl peroxide is a synthetic organic peroxide, a white powder with a bleaching and oxidizing action. It is also well known as an acne treatment.

In food it is listed as a bleach, used to whiten flour and some whey and cheese products.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved for certain foods.

name: Acetone peroxide
text:
Acetone peroxide is a synthetic organic peroxide made from acetone and hydrogen peroxide. It is a strong oxidizing agent and in pure form is unstable.

It has been used to bleach and mature flour.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK. In the US it is approved in flour and bread.

name: Calcium peroxide
text:
Calcium peroxide is an inorganic compound, a white or yellowish powder that releases oxygen. It is made industrially.

It is listed as a bleach and improving agent, used to strengthen dough and bleach flour in baking.

It is not approved in the EU or the UK, and approved in the US.

name: Argon
text:
Argon is an inert noble gas that makes up about 1% of the atmosphere. It is obtained industrially by distilling liquefied air. It is colourless, odourless and does not react with food.

It is used as a packaging gas, displacing oxygen in packs and containers to slow spoilage and oxidation, for example in packaged snacks, wine and prepared foods.

It is approved in the EU and in the UK, and not approved in the US.

name: Helium
text:
Helium is a light, inert noble gas. It is extracted from natural gas deposits and is colourless, odourless and non-reactive.

It is listed as a packaging gas, used to create an inert atmosphere or to detect leaks in packaging.

It is approved in the EU and in the UK. In the US it is approved as a processing aid.

name: Dichlorodifluoromethane
text:
Dichlorodifluoromethane is a synthetic chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) gas, once widely sold as a refrigerant under the name Freon-12. It was also used as an aerosol propellant.

It is listed as a packaging gas. CFCs damage the ozone layer, so their use has been phased out.

It is banned in all countries in compliance with the Montreal Protocol, though it is listed by the FDA as a substance added to food in the US.

name: Nitrogen
text:
Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless, inert gas that makes up about 78% of air. It is obtained industrially from liquefied air.

As a packaging gas it replaces oxygen in packs of crisps, coffee, nuts and wine, slowing oxidation and staling. It is also used as a propellant, for instance in whipped toppings.

It is approved in the EU, the UK and the US.

name: Nitrous oxide
text:
Nitrous oxide is a colourless gas with a faintly sweet smell, made industrially. It is also known as laughing gas and used in medicine as an anaesthetic.

In food it is a propellant, best known for whipped cream dispensers and aerosol cream, because it dissolves in fat and gives a light foam.

It is approved in the EU and in the UK. In the US it is approved in dairy.

name: Butane
text:
Butane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas obtained from natural gas and petroleum refining. It is easily liquefied under pressure.

It is used as a propellant in aerosol products. In the EU this is for vegetable oil pan sprays.

It is approved in the EU for vegetable oil pan spray, approved in the UK and approved in the US.

name: Isobutane
text:
Isobutane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas, an isomer of butane, obtained from natural gas and petroleum refining. It is easily liquefied under pressure.

It works as a propellant in aerosol products, such as cooking sprays.

It is approved in the EU for vegetable oil pan spray, approved in the UK and approved in the US.

name: Propane
text:
Propane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas obtained from natural gas and petroleum refining, widely known as a fuel. It is easily liquefied under pressure.

In food it is used as a propellant in aerosol products, for example sprays of oil for greasing baking pans.

It is approved in the EU for vegetable oil pan spray, approved in the UK and approved in the US.

name: Chloropentafluoroethane
text:
Chloropentafluoroethane is a synthetic chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) gas, formerly used as a refrigerant and aerosol propellant.

It is listed as a propellant. CFCs damage the stratospheric ozone layer and have been phased out worldwide.

It is banned in all countries in compliance with the Montreal Protocol, although the FDA lists it as a substance added to food in the US.

name: Octafluorocyclobutane
text:
Octafluorocyclobutane is a synthetic fully fluorinated gas, used in the past as an aerosol propellant and in industry.

It is listed as a propellant for foods such as whipped toppings.

It is banned in all countries in compliance with the Montreal Protocol, though the FDA lists it as a substance added to food in the US.

name: Oxygen
text:
Oxygen is the colourless, odourless gas that makes up about 21% of air. For industrial use it is obtained from liquefied air.

As a packaging gas it is used in some modified-atmosphere packs, for example to keep the red colour of fresh meat or to support fresh produce.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Hydrogen
text:
Hydrogen is the lightest gas, colourless and odourless, and flammable. It is produced industrially from natural gas or by splitting water.

It is listed as a packaging gas. In food technology it is also used in the hydrogenation of oils.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Acesulfame potassium
text:
Acesulfame potassium (acesulfame K) is a synthetic, calorie-free sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar. It is a white crystalline powder, stable at high temperatures.

It is used in soft drinks, desserts, chewing gum and tabletop sweeteners, often blended with other sweeteners such as aspartame.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Aspartame
text:
Aspartame is a synthetic, low-calorie sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar. It is a compound of two amino acids, aspartic acid and phenylalanine.

It is used in diet soft drinks, desserts, yoghurts, chewing gum and tabletop sweeteners. It loses sweetness when heated, so it is little used in baking.

Products containing it must carry a warning that they contain a source of phenylalanine, because it is harmful to people with phenylketonuria. It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Cyclamic acid and cyclamates
text:
Cyclamic acid and its sodium and calcium salts, known as cyclamates, are synthetic sweeteners roughly 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar. They have no calories.

They are used in soft drinks, tabletop sweeteners and desserts, and are often blended with saccharin.

They are approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for them.

name: Isomalt
text:
Isomalt, or isomaltitol, is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made from sucrose through enzymatic conversion and hydrogenation. It is about half as sweet as sugar and provides fewer calories.

It is used in sugar-free hard candies, chewing gum, chocolate and cough sweets, and does not promote tooth decay.

It is approved in the EU. In the EU, foods with large amounts of polyols must warn that excessive consumption may have a laxative effect.

name: Saccharin
text:
Saccharin and its sodium, potassium and calcium salts form one of the oldest synthetic sweeteners, about 300 to 500 times sweeter than sugar, with no calories. It can leave a slightly bitter aftertaste.

It is used in tabletop sweeteners, diet drinks, confectionery and in toothpaste and medicines.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Sucralose
text:
Sucralose (trichlorogalactosucrose) is a synthetic sweetener made from sucrose by replacing three hydroxyl groups with chlorine. It is about 600 times sweeter than sugar and provides no usable calories.

It is stable when heated, so it is used in drinks, baked goods, desserts and tabletop sweeteners.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Alitame
text:
Alitame is a synthetic high-intensity sweetener built from the amino acids aspartic acid and alanine. It is far sweeter than sugar, reportedly by roughly 2,000 times.

It is listed as a sweetener and has seen limited use in food production, mainly in some countries outside Europe.

No EU, UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Thaumatin
text:
Thaumatin is a mixture of sweet-tasting proteins extracted from the fruit of the West African katemfe plant (Thaumatococcus daniellii). It is several thousand times sweeter than sugar, with a slow onset and lingering sweetness.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer in chewing gum, desserts, drinks and in animal feed.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Glycyrrhizin
text:
Glycyrrhizin is the sweet-tasting compound extracted from the root of liquorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra). It is about 30 to 50 times sweeter than sugar and has a lingering liquorice flavour.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer in confectionery, particularly liquorice sweets, and in drinks and tobacco products.

No EU, UK or US approval status is recorded for it. Eating large amounts of liquorice is known to raise blood pressure in some people.

name: Neohesperidine dihydrochalcone
text:
Neohesperidine dihydrochalcone (neohesperidine DC) is a semi-synthetic sweetener made from a flavonoid found in bitter oranges. It is roughly 1,000 times sweeter than sugar, with a slow onset and a lingering, cooling aftertaste.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer, masking bitterness in drinks, chewing gum, dairy products and pharmaceuticals.

It is approved in the EU.

name: Steviol glycosides
text:
Steviol glycosides are sweet compounds, such as stevioside and rebaudioside A, extracted from the leaves of the stevia plant (Stevia rebaudiana), native to South America. They are about 200 to 300 times sweeter than sugar and have no calories.

They are used in soft drinks, dairy products, desserts and tabletop sweeteners. Some people notice a slightly bitter or liquorice-like aftertaste.

They are approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for them.

name: Neotame
text:
Neotame is a synthetic, low-calorie sweetener chemically related to aspartame. It is much sweeter than sugar, roughly 7,000 to 13,000 times, so only tiny amounts are needed.

It is used as a sweetener in drinks, desserts, chewing gum and baked goods.

It is recorded as approved in 2010, but the country or region is not specified.

name: Aspartame-acesulfame salt
text:
Aspartame-acesulfame salt is a synthetic sweetener formed by combining aspartame and acesulfame in a single salt. It is a white crystalline substance, sweeter than sugar and low in calories.

It is classed as a stabiliser, but it is used as a sweetener in drinks, chewing gum and confectionery. Like aspartame, it is a source of phenylalanine and is a concern for people with phenylketonuria.

It is approved in the EU.

name: Polyglycitol syrup
text:
Polyglycitol syrup is a mixture of polyols and sugar-alcohol polymers, made by hydrogenating starch hydrolysates, usually from corn or wheat starch. It is a thick, clear, sweet syrup, less sweet than sugar.

It is used as a sweetener and bulking agent in sugar-free confectionery and chewing gum.

It is approved in the EU. In the EU, foods rich in polyols must warn that excessive consumption may have a laxative effect.

name: Maltitol
text:
Maltitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made by hydrogenating maltose from starch. It is about 75 to 90 percent as sweet as sugar and has fewer calories. It is sold as crystals or as maltitol syrup.

It is used as a sweetener, humectant and stabiliser in sugar-free chocolate, chewing gum, baked goods and ice cream.

It is approved in the EU. In the EU, excessive consumption may have a laxative effect, and labels must say so.

name: Lactitol
text:
Lactitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) made by hydrogenating lactose, the sugar of milk. It is about 30 to 40 percent as sweet as sugar and provides fewer calories.

It is used as a sweetener and bulking agent in sugar-free sweets, chocolate, baked goods and ice cream. It is also used in medicine as a laxative.

It is approved in the EU. In the EU, foods with large amounts of polyols must warn of a possible laxative effect.

name: Xylitol
text:
Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) found in small amounts in fruit and vegetables and produced industrially from xylose, often from birch wood or corncobs. It is about as sweet as sugar with roughly 40 percent fewer calories.

It is used in sugar-free chewing gum, sweets and toothpaste, and is known not to promote tooth decay.

It is approved in the EU. In the EU, excessive consumption may have a laxative effect, and labels must say so. Xylitol is highly toxic to dogs.

name: Erythritol
text:
Erythritol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) found naturally in small amounts in some fruit and fermented foods. It is produced industrially by fermenting glucose. It is about 60 to 70 percent as sweet as sugar and has almost no calories.

It is used as a sweetener and bulking agent in sugar-free drinks, confectionery, chocolate and tabletop sweeteners, and has a mild cooling effect.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Advantame
text:
Advantame is a synthetic high-intensity sweetener chemically related to aspartame and neotame. It is extremely sweet, roughly 20,000 times sweeter than sugar, so only minute amounts are used.

It is used as a sweetener and flavour enhancer in drinks, desserts, chewing gum and confectionery.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.

name: Quillaia extract
text:
Quillaia extract is a natural extract from the bark of the soapbark tree (Quillaja saponaria), which grows in Chile and other parts of South America. It is rich in saponins, which act like soap.

It works as a foaming agent and emulsifier, giving a stable foam in soft drinks such as root beer and ginger beer, and is also used in some cosmetics.

It is approved in the EU. No UK or US approval status is recorded for it.
